title: Spooked

jokes.text: Chef from South Park. It's genius. Just some chef.
jokes.setup: Andy is pre-screening Halloween costumes and announces his own costume choice as if it's a profound insight
jokes.punchline: The 'genius' is that it's literally just a chef costume — the joke is its own anti-climax delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Works because it's pure Andy — grandiose self-satisfaction over something completely ordinary. The economy is great ('It's genius. Just some chef.') but it's a mild opener.

jokes.text: I have three simple rules: don't be offensive, don't be cliché, and don't take the first two rules too seriously.
jokes.setup: Andy announces he has three simple rules for Halloween costumes, implying reasonable authority
jokes.punchline: The third rule immediately undercuts his authority and renders the first two meaningless — pure self-contradiction
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-structured joke. The rule-then-anti-rule format is clean and the economy is excellent. Slightly generic in that it's a familiar comic structure, but executed well for an opening.

jokes.text: The gorilla from Rise of the Planet of the Apes. The one who sacrifices his life. Whoa! Spoiler alert. It's been out for ages, man.
jokes.setup: An employee describes their costume as the sacrificial gorilla from Rise of the Planet of the Apes
jokes.punchline: Andy reacts with 'Whoa! Spoiler alert!' — only for the employee to dismiss it as old news
jokes.explanation: Functional topical joke about spoiler culture. The reversal (Andy's indignation vs. the employee's dismissal) is fine but not especially sharp. Datedness weakens its longevity.

jokes.text: Why can't there just be two Kate Middletons?
jokes.setup: Someone's gorilla costume has been vetoed because Kevin allegedly already has a gorilla suit
jokes.punchline: Another employee complains about the unfairness — but their complaint is about being a duplicate Kate Middleton, which is its own absurd status flex
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny in how it implies the speaker was very invested in being Kate Middleton, but the joke doesn't build to anything sharp.

jokes.text: I stayed up all night and I watched that g.d. wedding and then I came to work and I made everyone else watch it all day.
jokes.setup: Discussion about who went to the Royal Wedding, implying Meredith was absent from work for the funeral
jokes.punchline: Meredith reveals she not only watched the wedding obsessively herself but forced the entire office to watch it — the compulsion is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good Meredith characterization — the compulsive, unfiltered behavior fits her perfectly. The escalation from 'I watched it' to 'I made everyone else watch' is the engine.

jokes.text: You're the people's princess! Diana was nothing!
jokes.setup: Meredith is defending her obsession with Kate Middleton to the office
jokes.punchline: She dismisses Princess Diana — a beloved figure — as 'nothing' compared to Kate Middleton, with unhinged conviction
jokes.explanation: This is a great Meredith moment — the absolute conviction and the specificity of targeting Diana make it genuinely surprising and funny. 'Diana was nothing!' is a perfectly absurd claim delivered with total commitment. High quotability, excellent economy, strong character integration.

jokes.text: I thought you were at your sister's funeral. What I said was 'My sister's funeral is this weekend.' Didn't say I'd be there.
jokes.setup: Colleague implies Meredith skipped work for a funeral
jokes.punchline: Meredith clarifies with lawyerly precision that she never committed to attending her own sister's funeral
jokes.explanation: This is excellent. The setup is clean (implied she was absent for a funeral), the punchline reveals something deeply dark about Meredith in a perfectly constructed two-beat: 'What I said was...' / 'Didn't say I'd be there.' The legal precision of the dodge is the heart of the joke. Perfect character integration — only Meredith could deliver this with zero shame. Highly quotable, structurally tight, genuinely dark without being mean-spirited.

jokes.text: Warms my heart thinking about them two kids... [pause] ...doing it.
jokes.setup: Meredith begins a seemingly warm, sentimental statement about the royal couple
jokes.punchline: The pause before '...doing it' reframes the entire statement as a creepy sexual observation
jokes.explanation: The strategic pause is the craft here — this is a classic misdirection structure and the transcript even marks it with a scene break to indicate the comic timing. Classic Meredith but the concept itself (dirty mind hiding behind wholesomeness) is not novel. Still lands well.

jokes.text: When they talk about all the nice things about dating a co-worker, they don't mention one of the best parts. After you're done dating, you still get to work together every single day.
jokes.setup: Jim does a talking head about the 'perks' of dating a co-worker
jokes.punchline: The supposed 'best part' is continuing to work with your ex — something universally regarded as awkward and terrible
jokes.explanation: Functional dry humor. Jim's deadpan makes it work, and it sets up the Erin/Andy tension of the episode, but it's not a particularly inventive observation. The irony is obvious once set up.

jokes.text: Kevin started crying, so I am Chris Bosh.
jokes.setup: Jim explains why he's wearing an NBA jersey costume — Darryl and Kevin needed a third for Three Kings
jokes.punchline: Jim's resistance crumbled entirely because Kevin cried, and the specific detail of 'Chris Bosh' (the odd man out of the Miami Heat trio) is perfectly chosen
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers: the absurdity of Kevin crying over a Halloween costume, and Jim being assigned Chris Bosh (not LeBron, not Wade — Bosh, the most forgettable of the trio). The economy is excellent and the Bosh specificity elevates what could be a throwaway.

jokes.text: What are you? Some kind of Jamaican zombie woman? / Ryan: Whoopi Goldberg. / Has no one here heard of Kerrigan from StarCraft?
jokes.setup: Angela is in costume as Kerrigan from the video game StarCraft — an obscure, elaborate sci-fi character
jokes.punchline: Andy guesses 'Jamaican zombie woman,' Ryan guesses 'Whoopi Goldberg' — the escalating wrongness of the guesses is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble moment. 'Whoopi Goldberg' as a guess is genuinely funny because Ryan clearly doesn't care and just throws out a famous Black woman's name. The escalation from confusion to more specific-yet-still-wrong answers rewards attention. Good character work for Angela as the unrecognized nerd.

jokes.text: It's all Toby's fault. Every Halloween, I tell him the same thing: you can't bring weapons into the office. And every year he says the same thing: 'As soon as I get my weapons back, I'm going to kill you.' But there I am at Thanksgiving, alive, you know? I'm a lucky turkey.
jokes.setup: Andy complains about Toby's annual Halloween weapons violation
jokes.punchline: The punchline is that Toby's annual death threat has become so routine Andy treats it as charming office tradition — and 'I'm a lucky turkey' is the perfect tag
jokes.explanation: Strong confessional bit. The rhythm of 'I tell him / he says / but there I am' is well-structured, and 'I'm a lucky turkey' is a genuinely delightful, quotable tag that earns its place. The dark undercurrent (Toby actually threatens his boss annually) adds depth.

jokes.text: I just got a text from Broccoli Rob. 'Boo!' It scared me. And then I got this text from Robert California: 'Looking forward to Halloween party. Expectations are high.' Scared the * out of me.
jokes.setup: Andy shows two texts that 'scared' him for Halloween
jokes.punchline: The first text (from Broccoli Rob, a joke character) is trivially spooky; Robert California's professional expectations text is genuinely terrifying to Andy
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup/punchline with a Halloween-appropriate misdirection structure. The juxtaposition is sharp: a literal 'Boo!' vs. the professional dread of a boss's expectations. The censored expletive adds comedic emphasis. Strong character integration for Andy as someone terrified of his boss.

jokes.text: G'day, Pameroo. Could you shoot this off for me? / Pam's reaction to Andy's random Australian accent.
jokes.setup: Andy approaches Pam at reception with a completely unprompted Australian accent
jokes.punchline: The transcript notes 'Australian accent' as if Pam is identifying what just happened to her — her deadpan processing of Andy's absurdity is the joke
jokes.explanation: Andy's random accent is a mild character beat. The humor is in Pam's bewildered acknowledgment. Not particularly inventive but consistent with the show's texture.

jokes.text: What are you doing? I just wanted to see how you do it. If you're doing something I don't...
jokes.setup: Erin catches Andy watching her work, apparently mimicking or studying her
jokes.punchline: Andy's explanation is half-finished and fumbling — it implies he's jealous of Erin but can't articulate why, setting up their uncomfortable dynamic
jokes.explanation: More cringe setup than punchline. The humor is in Andy's awkwardness but it doesn't land as a complete joke — it's transitional scene work.

jokes.text: One day he's like 'Fax these documents, please.' The next he's like, 'Pam, you fax them. Who cares what Erin's feeling.'
jokes.setup: Erin is doing a confessional about Andy's confusing hot-and-cold behavior toward her
jokes.punchline: The paraphrased Andy quote — 'Who cares what Erin's feeling' — is an absurd escalation that likely isn't what Andy said but reveals Erin's wounded interpretation
jokes.explanation: Good Erin character moment — her unreliable narration is itself funny. The fake quote is the joke, and it works because it tells us more about her emotional state than about Andy's actual behavior.

jokes.text: How would you rate me as a receptionist on a scale of one to three? Um... Two? It's like the second to last thing I wanted to hear.
jokes.setup: Erin asks Pam to rate her on a scale of one to three
jokes.punchline: Pam gives a 'two' (seemingly good) and Erin reveals it's 'the second to last thing I wanted to hear' — meaning she wanted a 'three' not a 'one', and 'two' is specifically disappointing
jokes.explanation: Clever joke that requires a beat of mental processing. The scale of one-to-three is already funny (why not ten?), and 'second to last thing I wanted to hear' is a precise, unexpected response that rewards thinking through the math. Good Erin characterization — enthusiastic but oddly particular.

jokes.text: Hey, if you go by the Banshee Pub, tell the Man in Black I say hello.
jokes.setup: Bob and Phyllis are going on a haunted walking tour and Meredith is reacting
jokes.punchline: Meredith casually mentions she has a personal relationship with a ghost — asking to relay a greeting — as if this is a completely normal social request
jokes.explanation: Great economy — the joke is entirely in the casualness of the delivery. Meredith asking to 'say hello' to a ghost as if he's an acquaintance is funny and sets up Pam's ghost story nicely.

jokes.text: Wait, they have food there?
jokes.setup: Pam is telling a serious ghost story about working at the Banshee Pub when a mysterious man appeared in the mirror
jokes.punchline: Someone interrupts the spooky story to ask if the bar has food — completely deflating the tension
jokes.explanation: The interruption is perfectly timed — it lands right as the ghost story is building. The mundane practicality of the question (food!) against the supernatural context is the joke. Great economy, though character assignment is unclear.

jokes.text: No. My wife does not believe in ghosts. [camera look implied]
jokes.setup: Pam has just told her ghost story to the office with evident belief
jokes.punchline: Jim's talking-head flatly contradicts his wife's beliefs — the camera look and deadpan denial is the joke, especially given their loving relationship
jokes.explanation: Classic Jim talking-head move — the cut to him categorically denying something the audience just saw Pam believe is a reliable Office formula. Works due to character integration and economy.

jokes.text: I saw a ghost. / What I'm saying is, do you ever wonder what it was? / It was a ghost. I told you this on like our first date. / Yeah, I had just told you about the day I met the Blue Angels. I figured you had to top it.
jokes.setup: Jim tries diplomatically to suggest rational explanations for Pam's ghost sighting; Pam is completely unmoved
jokes.punchline: Jim reveals he suspected she was embellishing on their first date to match his Blue Angels story — implying she may have invented a ghost to compete
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent joke because it recontextualizes Pam's entire ghost story in a single sentence. The Blue Angels detail is specific and funny on its own, and the implication that Pam invented a ghost story to impress Jim on their first date is both romantic and hilarious. Strong character integration — it works for both Jim and Pam specifically. Pam's flat 'I don't know what to tell you, Jim' is a perfect deadpan response.

jokes.text: Looks like we're under a Jack attack. / And you, on this day of fantasy, are a labourer.
jokes.setup: Robert California arrives at the Halloween party and addresses Andy
jokes.punchline: Robert's observation that Andy — as 'Chef from South Park' — is 'a labourer' on 'this day of fantasy' is delivered with Robert's signature pretentious cadence
jokes.explanation: Robert California's verbal style is always funny when contrasted with mundane office observations. 'On this day of fantasy, are a labourer' is perfectly in character. The callback to Andy's costume adds a layer.

jokes.text: Bert, this is a paper company.
jokes.setup: Robert California introduces his young son Bert to the office
jokes.punchline: After the grand introduction, he describes Dunder Mifflin to his son with zero enthusiasm as 'a paper company' — the deflation is everything
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — four words, enormous deflation. Robert's complete lack of pride in his own workplace, delivered with the same commanding register he uses for everything, is very funny. Perfect Robert California character work.

jokes.text: Can I use a computer? I need to check a hurricane.
jokes.setup: Robert's son Bert is introduced to the office as a kid at his dad's workplace
jokes.punchline: His first request is to check 'a hurricane' — a child's oddly specific and urgent meteorological concern
jokes.explanation: The joke is that 'I need to check a hurricane' sounds alarmingly urgent and specific — kids aren't usually hurricane-tracking. It sets up Bert as a mini-Robert California, and the payoff of Dwight and Bert bonding over weather disasters later makes this land better in hindsight.

jokes.text: Wow. Who shot our grownup party with the kiddy ray gun?
jokes.setup: Robert arrives to see the Halloween party is very child-friendly (pin the word on the witch, etc.)
jokes.punchline: Robert's line about a 'kiddy ray gun' is a hilariously sophisticated complaint about the lameness of the party
jokes.explanation: Robert California inventing the phrase 'kiddy ray gun' is exactly the kind of thing this character does — pompous, oddly specific, and weirdly evocative. It's original wordplay entirely in character. High quotability.

jokes.text: Now then, how are we today? / Fine. Great. / Just fine, Kelly? Everything all right? / Mm-hmm. / You feeling fulfilled in your life? / I guess. / You guess? So there is something you want that you do not have. Try not to think about it. Because it's too terrifying to imagine.
jokes.setup: Robert California turns small talk into an existential interrogation of Kelly
jokes.punchline: He identifies Kelly's latent dissatisfaction and tells her 'try not to think about it. Because it's too terrifying to imagine' — as if he's done her a favor
jokes.explanation: This is a strong Robert California scene because he weaponizes social pleasantries into existential horror. 'Try not to think about it. Because it's too terrifying to imagine.' as a follow-up to 'you guess?' is wonderfully cruel and perfectly in character. The escalation from small talk to existential dread is the comedy engine.

jokes.text: What is it, Kelly? What is this great fear of yours? / Never marrying. / Yes. Dying alone, that is very scary.
jokes.setup: Robert has been pressing Kelly to name her deepest fear
jokes.punchline: Kelly's fear is 'never marrying' — completely banal and specific to her character — and Robert treats it with the gravity of a Shakespearean tragedy
jokes.explanation: The callback completes the Kelly interrogation well. Kelly's answer is quintessentially Kelly (shallow, romantic, immediate), and Robert treating it with Shakespearean gravity is perfectly in character. The comedy comes from the tonal mismatch.

jokes.text: And how are you, Toby? / So great. [Robert stares; Toby visibly deteriorates]
jokes.setup: After the Kelly interrogation, Robert turns to Toby with the same existential small talk
jokes.punchline: Toby's 'So great' — probably a brave performance — is followed by visible discomfort under Robert's gaze. The joke is that Toby cannot withstand even a moment of Robert's attention.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the Kelly interrogation is immediately subverted — while Kelly broke down gradually, Toby's 'So great' implies he's already broken. The brevity of Toby's scene vs. Kelly's suggests Robert quickly gave up on him, which is its own joke. Strong character integration for both Robert and Toby.

jokes.text: Oh, I put those up. / I know. I'm taking them down. / I almost wonder if putting nothing on this wall is more Halloween-y.
jokes.setup: Angela is removing Erin's Halloween decorations from a wall
jokes.punchline: Angela rationalizes her removal as an aesthetic choice — 'nothing on this wall is more Halloween-y' — which is both passive-aggressive and genuinely absurdist
jokes.explanation: Good Angela moment — she's so controlling she rationalizes her bullying as artistic direction. The 'more Halloween-y' logic is delightfully tortured.

jokes.text: So can we speak our minds now? Or are we still sparing feelings? Because I hate all of this.
jokes.setup: The group is navigating party planning authority between Erin and the new helpers
jokes.punchline: Angela cuts through all the politics to declare she 'hates all of this' — classic Angela bluntness
jokes.explanation: Standard but effective Angela. 'Are we still sparing feelings?' is a good setup for the blunt punchline. Reliable character comedy.

jokes.text: Very low pressure in the Sargasso Sea. Warm air from South America. Cold air from Greenland. All signs point to the perfect storm. / Perfectly mediocre.
jokes.setup: Bert is analyzing weather data on the computer with genuine urgency while the party prep happens around him
jokes.punchline: Robert California's 'Perfectly mediocre' serves double duty — applying to the storm and to the party, deadpanned over his son's weather analysis
jokes.explanation: The double meaning of 'perfectly mediocre' (hurricane AND party) is a nice piece of writing. Bert's absurd hurricane expertise makes this work — the kid is a small Robert California, which is its own running joke.

jokes.text: If you had some really big wings with blades on the end, you'd kind of look like Kerrigan from StarCraft. / Damn it! I am Kerrigan from StarCraft. I've been censored.
jokes.setup: The Kerrigan costume confusion from earlier is revisited; Dwight (a known nerd) actually recognizes who she is
jokes.punchline: The employee's outrage at 'I've been censored' reveals the costume was supposed to have wings with blades — making the costume even more elaborate and the vetoing of it more absurd
jokes.explanation: Good callback that expands the earlier joke. 'I've been censored' for a Halloween costume is a funny escalation, and Dwight being the one person who recognizes the character (while also critiquing it) is perfect character integration.

jokes.text: If you're going to be a Zerg, at least be a lurker. Not some girl. / Kerrigan is ruler of the Zerg swarm. / Yeah. She also has boobs. / Yeah, but no nipples.
jokes.setup: Dwight and Angela are debating the costume merits of Angela's Kerrigan costume on StarCraft lore grounds
jokes.punchline: The argument escalates from lore accuracy to a debate about video game character anatomy — 'Yeah, but no nipples' is the perfect absurdist endpoint
jokes.explanation: This is a great Dwight/Angela exchange. The escalation from 'be a lurker not some girl' to a nipple debate is both unexpected and completely in character for both of them. 'Yeah, but no nipples' is genuinely funny as an argument-winning statement delivered with full seriousness. High quotability.

jokes.text: Hey, what's the jive with Angela and Phyllis helping with the party? / November's sure creeping up, ain't it? You can't stop that month.
jokes.setup: Darryl directly asks Andy why he brought in Angela and Phyllis to help Erin with the party
jokes.punchline: Andy completely dodges the question with a non-sequitur about November approaching — a politician's deflection delivered with fake philosophical weight
jokes.explanation: 'November's sure creeping up, ain't it? You can't stop that month.' is a wonderful non-answer. The specificity of November (not just 'time' or 'fall') and the gravity with which Andy says you 'can't stop that month' is funny. Pure panic deflection in character.

jokes.text: I'm throwing the Halloween party and I just want to amp it up. I think it could use some extra pizzazz. Okay. Where does Gabe factor in?
jokes.setup: Erin goes to Gabe — her creepy ex — for help making the party scarier and sexier
jokes.punchline: Gabe's 'Where does Gabe factor in?' in the third person is both pitiable and oblivious — he immediately makes Erin's request about his feelings
jokes.explanation: Gabe speaking in the third person about himself is a nice character touch — it's pathetic and funny. The pivot from Erin's practical request to Gabe's emotional agenda is a good cringe beat.

jokes.text: Remember that Halloween party you took me to once? The one where I started crying as soon as I walked in and I didn't stop crying?
jokes.setup: Erin is asking Gabe to help recreate the atmosphere of a past Halloween party
jokes.punchline: The party she's describing as a model was one where she cried the entire time — implying 'good scary' and 'traumatizing' are the same to her
jokes.explanation: Good Erin moment — she recounts trauma with fondness because she genuinely doesn't distinguish between 'exciting scary' and 'traumatized crying.' Very much in character.

jokes.text: I will make this sexier than you could ever imagine. / No, just scary.
jokes.setup: Erin asks Gabe for help making the party 'more adult, more scary and sexy'
jokes.punchline: Gabe immediately zeroes in on 'sexy' and offers to make it 'sexier than you could ever imagine' — which is deeply uncomfortable given he's her ex
jokes.explanation: Classic Gabe creepiness. His laser-focus on 'sexy' and the grandiosity of 'sexier than you could ever imagine' is perfectly pathetic. Erin's flat correction ('No, just scary') is the clean punchline.

jokes.text: Pam Halpert. Hey. It's Jim Halpert. I was wondering if you wanted to see a movie tonight. / Is it called Ghostbusters? / It's called Ghostbusters.
jokes.setup: Jim calls Pam as if they are strangers, apparently roleplaying their first date scenario to address the ghost debate
jokes.punchline: Pam immediately knows exactly what movie he's 'suggesting' — Ghostbusters — and Jim confirms it, defeated
jokes.explanation: A sweet and funny Jim/Pam moment. The bit of him using their full names on a call is charming, and Pam's instant Ghostbusters prediction (without hesitation) reveals both how well she knows him and how obvious his plan was. The flat 'It's called Ghostbusters' confirmation is the perfect beat. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: I ain't afraid of no ghosts. [Jim to camera]
jokes.setup: After the Ghostbusters phone call, Jim looks at the camera
jokes.punchline: Quoting Ghostbusters directly to camera — acknowledging his own plan while playing along with the show's format
jokes.explanation: A quick, fun camera moment but it's riding entirely on the pre-existing Ghostbusters quote. Economy is perfect (one line), but it's not original — it's a reference. Works as a button to the previous joke.

jokes.text: Dwight, are you eating a stick? / It's a root, idiot.
jokes.setup: Jim notices Dwight gnawing on something in the Halloween party scene
jokes.punchline: Dwight clarifies with contempt — it's a root, not a stick — as if this distinction is obviously important and Jim is the fool for not knowing
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy for a classic Dwight bit. The correction 'It's a root, idiot' — where the correction is itself absurd (eating a root is not better than eating a stick) but Dwight treats it as a crucial distinction — is perfectly in character. Short and sharp.

jokes.text: Everyone hates you. / That's really rude. / I don't tell you hurricanes suck, even though it's true. / What do you like, tornadoes? Try influenza.
jokes.setup: After the stick/root exchange, Dwight turns his attention to Bert and his hurricane obsession
jokes.punchline: Dwight dismisses hurricanes as inferior to influenza — the escalation from personal insult to meteorological/epidemiological debate is absurdly funny
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's better jokes. 'Try influenza' is a great punchline — completely unexpected, deeply Dwight (his survivalist expertise), and the debate over the 'best' natural disaster/disease is absurd and characterful. 'Everyone hates you' as a greeting to a child is a good setup.

jokes.text: I suppose you're going to tell me the scariest animal is a shark. / Try box jellyfish.
jokes.setup: The Dwight/Bert natural disaster debate continues into dangerous animals
jokes.punchline: Dwight preempts the expected 'shark' answer and corrects to 'box jellyfish' — continuing his pattern of dismissing conventional wisdom for obscure accuracy
jokes.explanation: Strong continuation of the Dwight/Bert dynamic. 'Try box jellyfish' has the same energy as 'try influenza' — Dwight consistently one-upping with obscure correct answers. The running gag of these two finding common ground through esoteric knowledge is good character work.

jokes.text: I'm only scared of real things, like serial killers and kidnappers. Not things that don't exist like ghosts or mummies.
jokes.setup: Jim declares he's only afraid of 'real things' like serial killers
jokes.punchline: He lists 'mummies' as something that doesn't exist — which prompts an immediate factual correction
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the mummy correction — Jim's confident irrationality (serial killers are scarier than ghosts, but mummies are fake?) creates the comedic trap he's about to fall into.

jokes.text: Mummies are real. There are mummies at museums.
jokes.setup: Jim lists mummies as things that 'don't exist'
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately and correctly points out that mummies are real and available for viewing at museums
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dwight. He's being completely factual and the joke is that he's RIGHT — and Jim's embarrassed silence follows. 'They're all over.' is a great, casual tag.

jokes.text: Why on Earth would a museum put a mummy in it?
jokes.setup: Dwight has correctly established that mummies exist and are in museums; Jim is backed into a corner
jokes.punchline: Jim's response is to question why museums would display mummies — doubling down on his confusion in a way that makes no sense, revealing his embarrassment
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff of the mummy exchange and it's great — Jim, usually the straight man, is caught being wrong and responds by saying something even MORE wrong. 'Why on Earth would a museum put a mummy in it?' implies he believes museums are mummy-free zones, and the line is delivered (presumably) with genuine wounded logic. A nice inversion of Jim's usual role.

jokes.text: A little witch's brew? I grew this party up real fast. Get out of here, little kid party. Nobody loves you. And clean up your room. Grownups are going to use it later.
jokes.setup: The party has been transformed from child-friendly to adult-scary; Phyllis is presiding over the new version
jokes.punchline: Phyllis addressing the 'little kid party' as if dismissing an actual child is delightfully unhinged — 'clean up your room, grownups are going to use it later' is a perfect escalation
jokes.explanation: Phyllis breaking the fourth wall to speak to an abstract concept (the kid party) as if it's a real child is inventive. The line 'clean up your room, grownups are going to use it later' is especially funny. Good for a character who usually stays in the background.

jokes.text: The party looks fun, doesn't it? Everybody seems to be in there having a great time. So maybe now would be a great time for me to pop back on the computer. / I'm using it. I'm about to play StarCraft with him.
jokes.setup: Angela attempts to reclaim the computer by pointing out the party is going well and she doesn't need to monitor it
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals he's about to play StarCraft with Bert — two extremely unlikely companions bonding over video games
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Dwight/Bert dynamic — of course they ended up bonding over StarCraft. Angela's passive-aggressive attempts to get her computer back being foiled by a child is good secondary comedy.

jokes.text: Pam, do you think anyone's going to notice I've worn this costume before when I wasn't pregnant? You know, I guess nobody would believe it still fits.
jokes.setup: A character reveals they're recycling a Halloween costume, hoping no one notices
jokes.punchline: The joke is that the costume 'fitting' while pregnant is what's implausible — implying it was a tight fit before and somehow still works pregnant, or the reverse
jokes.explanation: A mild gag — the self-deprecating joke about body size/pregnancy fitting into a costume. Contextually it's likely a brief laugh. Not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, I'm an Oscar Liar Wiener!
jokes.setup: Kevin announces his Halloween costume
jokes.punchline: He's dressed as an 'Oscar Meyer Wiener' (hot dog) but says 'Oscar Liar Wiener' — either he's mispronounced it or is commenting on Oscar being a liar (a joke about Oscar's office persona)
jokes.explanation: The wordplay is sharp — 'Oscar Liar Wiener' works on multiple levels: Kevin dressed as a hot dog, the Oscar Meyer brand name, and Oscar (Martinez) being called a liar. Kevin's delivery would be triumphant and proud, adding to the comedy. 'I'm an Oscar Liar Wiener!' as a big reveal is inherently funny.

jokes.text: The Cinema of the Unsettling is a growing film movement. The most well-known film in the genre is an hour-long shot of a squirrel with diarrhea.
jokes.setup: Gabe introduces his 'scary' film contribution to the party by explaining the 'Cinema of the Unsettling'
jokes.punchline: The flagship film of this pompous cinematic movement is 'an hour-long shot of a squirrel with diarrhea'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The setup perfectly captures pretentious art-house culture (a 'growing film movement'), and then completely demolishes it with one of the most specific, disgusting, and perfectly chosen examples imaginable. 'An hour-long shot of a squirrel with diarrhea' is exactly the right length of time and exactly the right subject matter — specific enough to be vivid, absurd enough to be hilarious. It is completely in character for Gabe (pretentious, intense, oblivious to social norms). Highly quotable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — in fact exceeds it due to the extraordinary specificity and originality of the punchline.

jokes.text: Is that my grandmother? / There is no story. / Yeah, seems like there isn't a narrative. / Maybe the filmmaker realized that even narrative is comforting.
jokes.setup: The office watches Gabe's unsettling film, which apparently shows someone's grandmother
jokes.punchline: Gabe defends the lack of narrative with a pompous art-school explanation while everyone is horrified
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the Cinema of the Unsettling bit. 'Even narrative is comforting' is a perfectly pompous art-student line, and 'Is that my grandmother?' grounds the absurdity in the real horror of the situation. The gap between Gabe's seriousness and everyone's discomfort is the engine.

jokes.text: Is that my grandmother? / What's the story? / There is no story. / Yeah, seems like there isn't a narrative. / Maybe the filmmaker realized that even narrative is comforting.
jokes.setup: People are watching the unsettling film and trying to make sense of it
jokes.punchline: Gabe defends the lack of narrative as an artistic choice — 'even narrative is comforting' — while someone sees what might be their grandmother in the film
jokes.explanation: 'Is that my grandmother?' is a great background joke — the film is so disturbing and reality-adjacent that someone sees a family member in it. 'Even narrative is comforting' is a perfect art-pretension line from Gabe. The exchange works as a comedy of incompatible worldviews.

jokes.text: What the hell is going on here? / Okay, I think we've seen enough. You can turn it off now. / Kill it. / How'd you get in my car?
jokes.setup: The office watches Gabe's disturbing film until Robert California arrives
jokes.punchline: 'How'd you get in my car?' — implies the film showed something involving someone's car, adding another layer of personal violation to the horror
jokes.explanation: 'How'd you get in my car?' is genuinely surprising — it implies Gabe has been filming people without their knowledge and the content is becoming personally intrusive. The escalation from general horror to personal violation is well-structured.

jokes.text: This game is called 'Pecker Poker.' It's the game of cards that gets you hard.
jokes.setup: After the film disaster, Gabe tries another contribution to the adult party
jokes.punchline: He pulls out 'Pecker Poker' — a woodpecker-themed card game — presenting it with a straight face as if this is a normal adult party game
jokes.explanation: The double entendre of 'Pecker Poker' (woodpecker card game vs. sexual connotation) and the tagline 'the game that gets you hard' is delivered by Gabe with presumably complete earnestness. The specificity of this being a real woodpecker card game makes it funnier than a purely sexual joke.

jokes.text: What we have here is a classic misunderstanding. Why didn't you simply ask Andy to clarify? Asking is a very easy thing to do. The two of you are obviously very close.
jokes.setup: Robert California has watched Erin and Gabe create a disaster of a party due to miscommunication; they're clearly ex-es with tension
jokes.punchline: 'The two of you are obviously very close' — delivered with full knowledge of their awkward ex status, twisting the knife
jokes.explanation: Robert's passive-aggressive observation is perfectly calibrated. 'Asking is a very easy thing to do' is condescending without being overtly cruel, and 'obviously very close' is dry irony given what we've just watched. Classic Robert California.

jokes.text: All I knew is that you wanted to have a talk with me at the end of the day, and I got nervous, so... / Did you think I was going to fire you? / No, I wasn't.
jokes.setup: Andy had planned to have a serious talk with Erin about their relationship; Erin derailed the party trying to impress him
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Erin panicked about being fired — and Andy's incredulous 'did you think I was going to fire you?' — followed by Erin's defensive 'No, I wasn't' (clearly a lie)
jokes.explanation: Good cringe payoff for the Andy/Erin tension. Erin's transparent denial is charming and very in character. The moment is more sweet than funny, though.

jokes.text: She's never come by, so. And she's never called here. / Unless it's your mom. / No, I didn't want her to call because I thought it would be weird, but now it's weird that she's not calling.
jokes.setup: Andy explains his new relationship to Erin — noting his girlfriend has never called the office
jokes.punchline: Erin suggests 'unless it's your mom,' which is a sharp little dig, and Andy's continued reasoning about the weirdness of calling vs. not calling is anxious comedy
jokes.explanation: 'Unless it's your mom' is a mild but effective dig from Erin that lands on Andy's obliviousness. The Andy meta-commentary about calling being weird is anxious character comedy but a bit drawn out.

jokes.text: Two dates? / Three dates? / Thirty-one. / Wow. / I'm so happy for you guys. Um. Let me know when you get to 40.
jokes.setup: Andy reveals he's been on 31 dates with his new girlfriend; Erin guesses progressively higher
jokes.punchline: Erin's response to 'thirty-one' — 'I'm so happy for you guys. Let me know when you get to 40' — is a perfect performance of forced cheerfulness hiding genuine pain
jokes.explanation: 'Let me know when you get to 40' is a great line — it's Erin being supportive on the surface while the specificity of 'when you get to 40' reveals she's already dreading each milestone. The guesses (Two? Three?) vs. the answer (Thirty-one) create a comic reveal. Good character work for Erin.

jokes.text: I just don't get it, Pam. You're a rational person. / Thank you. / Jim doesn't let me wash his NFL jersey during the playoffs. How is this any less logical?
jokes.setup: Meredith is defending Pam's belief in ghosts
jokes.punchline: She compares ghost belief to Jim's jersey superstition — and the argument is actually pretty solid, which makes it funny
jokes.explanation: Meredith making a surprisingly cogent philosophical argument about superstition is funny in itself — she's not supposed to be the reasonable one. Jim's defensive response ('it's not like I think that's going to help the Eagles win') undercuts his own earlier skepticism.

jokes.text: Maybe the Eagles will hear about it and want to play better.
jokes.setup: Jim defends his jersey superstition by saying it's a 'collective thing'
jokes.punchline: He then explains that 'maybe the Eagles will hear about it and want to play better' — which is exactly the magical thinking he was mocking in Pam
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Jim's rational man position — he's exposed as exactly as superstitious as Pam, just about sports. 'Maybe the Eagles will hear about it and want to play better' is a perfect self-own that he doesn't recognize as such.

jokes.text: Exactly. Thank you. Go! Get up there right now.
jokes.setup: Jim has just revealed his jersey logic ('maybe the Eagles will hear about it') which perfectly validates Pam's ghost belief
jokes.punchline: Pam and Meredith immediately use it as a victory — 'Exactly. Thank you. Go!'
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat to cap the ghost debate. The comedy is in the reversal — Jim is now losing this argument. Functions as a button more than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Is she Asian? / I don't know. She's from somewhere, I bet. / Did Andy say his girlfriend's from the forest? / I don't know, Phyllis. Maybe she's from the city.
jokes.setup: Angela and Phyllis are speculating about Andy's mystery girlfriend
jokes.punchline: 'She's from somewhere, I bet' is the epitome of useless speculation, and 'from the forest' is a hilariously specific misinterpretation
jokes.explanation: Phyllis mishearing something as 'forest' is a funny character bit — she often mishears or misunderstands, and 'she's from somewhere, I bet' is perfectly dim speculation from Angela. Mild but consistent with the show's texture.

jokes.text: Looks terribly real, doesn't it, Creed? / No. / Are you scared of snakes? / You don't live as long as I have without a healthy fear of snakes, Bobby.
jokes.setup: Dwight is showing off what appears to be a fake snake prop at the Halloween party
jokes.punchline: Creed denies it looks real, then reveals his own ancient wisdom about snake fear — addressed to 'Bobby' (presumably Dwight) — suggesting a long personal history with snakes
jokes.explanation: Creed's 'you don't live as long as I have without a healthy fear of snakes, Bobby' is a great Creed line — cryptic, implying a storied and possibly criminal past, and mildly threatening. 'Bobby' for 'Dwight' is also a small mystery. High quotability for Creed content.

jokes.text: Yeah, I guess sometimes I have nightmares about being buried alive.
jokes.setup: The conversation about fears is ongoing; Jim contributes his
jokes.punchline: Jim's fear ('being buried alive') is both unexpectedly specific and genuinely relatable, delivered with Jim's characteristic casual understatement
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat but not a fully-formed joke. The deadpan admission is funny but it's a mild observational comment rather than a constructed comedic moment.

jokes.text: Honestly, Jim gives me the creeps.
jokes.setup: The conversation about fears is ongoing; Creed contributes an unsolicited opinion about Jim
jokes.punchline: Creed — who is objectively the most disturbing person in the office — finds JIM creepy
jokes.explanation: This is a fantastic Creed line. The inversion — Creed, who clearly has a criminal past and gives everyone the creeps, being the one to find Jim unsettling — is a perfect use of the character. Maximum economy (six words), perfect character integration, and genuinely surprising. Creed lines work best when they're unexplained and this is a prime example.

jokes.text: Like a few years down the road, Cece says 'Mom, there's a ghost in my closet.' Now you say one of two things: One, 'You're just having a bad dream.' Or two, 'Let's go see what it wants.'
jokes.setup: Jim frames the ghost debate as a parenting question — what do you tell your daughter if she says there's a ghost?
jokes.punchline: 'Let's go see what it wants' — the second option treats the ghost as a guest with needs and a personality, which is absurdly specific
jokes.explanation: 'Let's go see what it wants' is the joke — treating a ghost as a visitor with intentions and needs. The specificity of 'what it wants' vs. something like 'let's check it out' is the craft. Good Jim/Pam parenting debate setup.

jokes.text: Dwight's extended ghost story — beginning with the suicide house and Lydia, escalating to a snake in a crib full of dirt, embalmed bodies rising from sarcophagi, 'for they were mummies,' then pivoting to Lydia's failed marriage, and concluding with the baby saying 'I'm fine, bitch. I'm fine.'
jokes.setup: Dwight begins telling a ghost story to resolve the Jim/Pam ghost debate
jokes.punchline: The story starts as a spooky tale, escalates to include snakes, mummies, and supernatural horror, then completely pivots to being about a failed marriage and emotional withdrawal — culminating in the baby saying 'I'm fine, bitch. I'm fine.'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic centerpiece and one of the great Dwight monologues. The joke operates on multiple levels: (1) it begins as a conventional ghost story, (2) escalates absurdly with snakes and mummies, (3) seamlessly pivots to a metaphor about Jim and Pam's relationship (the 'man, Tall, slim. Jim' description, sleeping one inch farther apart, Lydia leaving), (4) turns into a thinly-veiled character assassination of Pam ('quit the book club, the choir, citing their high expectations'), and (5) resolves with the baby saying 'I'm fine, bitch' — subverting all expectations simultaneously. The 'for they were mummies' callback to the earlier mummy debate is excellent structural work. The whole thing is extraordinarily specific and entirely in Dwight's voice. Among the best Dwight monologues in the series.

jokes.text: She thought: 'Wait, I don't have a husband.' For Lydia and her husband had had an argument one they couldn't get past. Each night they slept one inch farther apart until one night Lydia left.
jokes.setup: Dwight's ghost story has fully pivoted to being about Pam and Jim's marriage
jokes.punchline: The horror-story framing is completely abandoned in favor of a sincere and cutting portrait of a marriage dissolving through slow emotional withdrawal — sleeping one inch farther apart is a genuinely poetic and sad image delivered as horror
jokes.explanation: Part of the larger ghost story sequence (Joke #59) but distinct enough to stand alone as the emotional core. 'Each night they slept one inch farther apart' is a genuinely striking image — it's almost too real and specific for a ghost story, which is why it's so funny and unsettling. Dwight delivering relationship insight this precise is the joke's engine, and it's remarkably well-written for a show in its eighth season.

jokes.text: Her lips slowly grew together from disuse. Every time she wanted to act, and didn't, another part of her face hardened until it was stone.
jokes.setup: The ghost story continues to catalog Pam's emotional decay
jokes.punchline: Dwight has now invented physical symptoms of emotional repression: lips growing together, face hardening to stone — treating Pam's passivity as a literal deformity
jokes.explanation: The most poetic and original image in the episode. 'Lips slowly grew together from disuse' as a metaphor for Pam's self-silencing, rendered as gothic body horror, is extraordinary writing. It operates simultaneously as dark comedy, character insight, and legitimate literary metaphor. The specificity ('every time she wanted to act, and didn't') shows Dwight has a terrifyingly accurate read on Pam's psychology. Possibly the best single image in the episode.

jokes.text: Baby sat up slowly, turned to mother, and said: 'I'm fine, bitch. I'm fine.'
jokes.setup: Dwight's increasingly surreal and personal ghost story reaches its climax — Pam rushes to the nursery to check on her baby
jokes.punchline: Baby speaks, delivering the punchline in the most unexpected register possible: pure street profanity from an infant, completely deflating the gothic tension
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best cold-structure comedy deliveries in The Office's run. The entire ghost story — over two minutes of careful escalation — exists entirely to set up the moment an infant says 'I'm fine, bitch.' The punchline works because: (1) the register shift from gothic horror to street profanity is maximally unexpected, (2) 'I'm fine' is the most complete contradiction of the elaborate horror scenario, (3) 'bitch' from a baby is inherently absurd, (4) the repetition of 'I'm fine' gives it perfect comedic rhythm. It's earned every single step of the way. Near-perfect joke construction. Extremely high quotability — this line alone justifies the entire two-minute build.

jokes.text: Fear plays an interesting role in our lives. How dare we let it motivate us? How dare we let it into our decision making? Into our livelihoods. Into our relationships. It's funny, isn't it? We take a day a year to dress up in costume and celebrate fear.
jokes.setup: Robert California delivers a closing monologue about fear
jokes.punchline: The grandeur of the speech vs. the mundane context (office Halloween party) — and 'how dare we' is an absurdly combative framing for an observation
jokes.explanation: Robert California's pretentious monologue is in character but functions more as a dramatic device than a joke. The comedy comes from the gap between the speech's weight and the setting. Moderate impact.

jokes.text: Toby. Hey, Bert. Want to see the dance? / Dem bones, dem bones, dem dry... / You're fired. / What? You heard me. Pack your things. / What? You can't— Gabe? Are you— I'm the CEO's son. / Pack your things. You're done.
jokes.setup: Toby, trying to connect with Robert's son Bert, offers to do the skeleton dance
jokes.punchline: Bert fires Toby — 'You're fired. Pack your things. You're done.' — and Toby's shock ('I'm the CEO's son') followed by Gabe enforcing the child's decision is the escalating absurdity
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode closer. Everything converges: Bert (the mini-Robert), Toby (the eternal punching bag), Gabe (the hapless enforcer), and the skeleton dance callback. Bert firing Toby — and Gabe immediately enforcing it without question — is a beautiful absurdist escalation. Toby's incredulous 'I'm the CEO's son' (meaning Bert, not himself) as a defense before realizing it's the CEO's son FIRING him is a great comic beat. The callback to the 'dem bones' dance makes the ending feel earned. Structurally excellent.

tmdb_overview: Erin works to make a spooky, non-childish Halloween party with help from Gabe. Dwight becomes friends with Robert's son, and Pam and Jim debate the existence of ghosts. Meanwhile, Robert tries to figure out everyone's deepest fears.
